text:
Today we open the doors of Moien Vëlo in Bertrange.

We make electric bikes that are slow on purpose. Our motors stop helping well before the legal limit, because a slower bike gives you more time to see, steer and stop.

We don't want to get you there fast. We want to get you there alive.

The kettle is on and the test bikes are charged. Do drop in.

#Luxembourg #Cycling

About Moien Vëlo

Moien Vëlo is a small Luxembourg company. We make e-bikes for people who'd like to keep cycling without rushing. Our bikes are slow on purpose. The motor stops helping well below the legal limit, because a slower bike gives you more time to see, steer and stop.

We're based in Bertrange. That's where you'll find our showroom, our workshop and, usually, a pot of coffee.

Visit our showroom

Our showroom in Bertrange is open Tuesday to Saturday, 10:00 to 18:00. Come in for a free test ride, a chat with our mechanics or simply a cup of coffee. There's step-free access, parking at the door and a flat test track at the back, away from traffic.

Delivery and set-up

We bring your new bike to your home anywhere in Luxembourg, free of charge. We set the saddle, handlebars and brake levers to fit you. Then we stay for a first short ride on your own street.

Steady Start lesson

Every new bike comes with a free one-hour Steady Start lesson. We'll show you how to set off, use the assist levels, brake on a slope and use walk assist. Lessons take place at our showroom, at whatever pace suits you.

Free first service

Three months after you take delivery, bring your bike in for a free first service. We check the brakes, gears, tyres, battery and lights, and tighten anything that has settled. It takes about an hour, and there's coffee while you wait.

Warranty

Every Moien Vëlo bike has a two-year warranty on the frame, motor and parts. The battery has a three-year warranty. If something goes wrong, bring the bike to us and we'll put it right.

Is an electric bike still exercise?

Yes. You always pedal; the motor adds to your effort rather than replacing it. On lower assist levels you'll work harder, and on higher ones less. How much exercise you get is up to you, and nobody is checking.

How long does the battery take to charge?

About four to five hours from empty, using the charger supplied. Many riders charge overnight or while they have lunch. You can top up at any time; there's no need to run the battery down first.

Do I need a licence?

No. Our motors are limited to 250 W and stop helping below 25 km/h. That means our bikes count as bicycles, so you don't need a licence or registration. We do suggest checking that your home insurance covers your bike against theft.

Should I wear a helmet?

We strongly recommend wearing a helmet on every ride, however short and however slow. We'll help you choose a comfortable one and adjust it properly when you collect your bike.

What happens at the first service?

After three months, bring your bike in for a free first service. We check and adjust the brakes, gears, tyres, battery and lights, and tighten anything that has settled during the first weeks of riding. It takes about an hour.

Do you deliver outside Luxembourg?

For now, we only deliver within Luxembourg. Many of our customers live across the border. They collect their bikes from our showroom in Bertrange, and we set each bike up for them before they leave.

Can I use my bike on cycle paths?

Yes. The motor stops helping below 25 km/h, so our bikes count as normal bicycles and may use cycle paths in Luxembourg. Please ride with care on paths shared with walkers. At our speeds, that comes naturally.

Meet the Stroller, our first e-bike.

Its motor helps you up to 15 km/h and then politely steps aside. The frame is low, so you step through rather than swing a leg over. Hydraulic disc brakes stop you smoothly, and the lights are built in.

It's €2,690, and a test ride costs nothing but a little of your time.

#Luxembourg #Cycling

Stroller

The Stroller is our everyday town bike. Step through the low frame, set off with a gentle push, and the motor helps you along up to 15 km/h. It's ideal for the market, the post office or a friend's house across town.

Range: up to 60 km. Weight: 24 kg. Price: €2,690.

The Sunday Best is for longer, gentler outings. It sits you upright, helps you along at up to 18 km/h and goes up to 80 km on a full charge.

That's far enough for lunch in Echternach and a slow ride home. We can't promise you'll burn off the dessert, but you will have pedalled.

#Luxembourg #Cycling

Sunday Best

An upright comfort tourer for longer, gentler outings. You sit tall, see the road ahead and let the motor help you along at up to 18 km/h. The 500 Wh battery takes you up to 80 km, far enough for lunch in the next valley and a slow ride home.

Weight: 26 kg. Price: €3,450.

Welcome to our first newsletter

Thank you for signing up. Once a month we'll write to you with a gentle ride to try, a tip for looking after your bike and news from the showroom. We won't write more often than that, and we won't shout.

A word about who we are. Moien Vëlo makes electric bikes that are slow on purpose. Our motors stop helping at 15 or 18 km/h, well below the legal limit of 25 km/h. A slower bike needs less distance to stop, and it gives you more time to look around.

We don't want to get you there fast. We want to get you there alive.

Until next month,
The team at Moien Vëlo

A customer asked us this week whether riding a Moien Vëlo bike counts as exercise.

You pedal. The motor helps. You arrive looking pleasantly windswept rather than exhausted. We think that counts, and we won't tell anyone how much the motor did.

Exercise, or something very like it.

A small safety habit for spring: check your tyres before each ride.

Press the tyre with your thumb. If it gives more than a little, add air. The right pressure makes steering steadier and braking more predictable.

If you'd rather not do it yourself, bring the bike in and we'll show you how.

Marguerite, from Mersch, bought a Stroller in March. She rides it to the market every Saturday.

'I used to drive two kilometres for bread,' she told us. 'Now I take the long way round and stop to talk to people.'

We like that she takes the long way. That's rather the point.

#Luxembourg

This month's ride: Mersch to Lintgen along the Alzette

Distance: about 8 km each way. Gradient: almost none. Café stops: at least one.

The cycle path follows the river through meadows and past old mills. It's quiet on weekday mornings, and the surface is good all the way. Start at Mersch station, where there's parking, and turn round whenever you've had enough.

On a Stroller or a Sunday Best, the round trip uses only a small part of a full battery, so there's no need to worry about range. Worry instead about which pastry to choose.

This Saturday we're leading a slow ride along the Alzette from Mersch to Lintgen. About 8 km, flat, with a coffee stop halfway.

Bring your own bike or borrow one of ours. We'll ride at the pace of the slowest rider, which is usually one of us.

Meet at 10:00 at the station car park.

Servicing and repairs

Our workshop services and repairs every model we sell. We recommend a check-up once a year, or every 1,500 km, whichever comes first. Book by phone or drop in at the showroom in Bertrange.

Why do our bikes stop helping at 15 or 18 km/h when the law allows 25?

Because a slower bike needs less distance to stop. You have more time to notice a pothole, a dog or a grandchild running out from a gate. You also have more time to enjoy the hedgerows.

We didn't build a slow bike by accident. We built it on purpose.

Looking after your battery

Your battery is the most expensive part of your bike, so a few habits are worth knowing.

Charge it indoors, at room temperature. Don't leave it empty for long. If you're not riding for a few weeks, charge it to around half and top it up once a month. Keep it out of direct sun on hot days and bring it inside on cold nights.

If it ever looks damaged or swollen, or feels unusually warm, stop using it and call us. That's rare, but it's the one battery rule that really matters.

The battery has a three-year warranty, so if something isn't right, we'll sort it out.

Summer riding advice from people who are in no hurry:

Ride in the morning, before the heat. Carry water. Put sun cream on your neck and arms. And stop at the first café that looks friendly.

The bike will wait. So will the view.

Meet the mechanics

Luc and Sandrine build, check and service every bike we sell. Between them they have more than forty years of experience with bicycles, from racing bikes to cargo bikes.

They'll tell you that the most important parts of any bike are the brakes, the tyres and the person riding it. Their job is the first two. For the third, there's the Steady Start lesson.

When your bike comes in for a service, they're the people who'll look after it. Do say hello.

Every new Moien Vëlo bike comes with a free one-hour Steady Start lesson.

We'll show you how to set off, how the assist levels feel and how to brake on a slope. We go at your pace, and most people are riding with confidence by the end of the hour.

Book yours when you collect your bike.

A ride with Marguerite

Marguerite bought one of our first Strollers in March. We asked if we could join her Saturday ride to the market in Mersch, and she agreed on one condition: we wouldn't rush her.

We needn't have worried. The ride took twenty minutes, of which perhaps eight were spent cycling and the rest talking to people she met on the way. She showed us the bench where she stops to watch the river, and the baker who keeps a loaf for her.

'I could drive,' she said. 'But then I wouldn't see anyone.'

We rode home slowly, as instructed.

Things our customers tell us they do on a Moien Vëlo bike:

Read the street names. Wave at neighbours. Notice a bakery they'd never seen. Smell the lime trees.

Things they haven't told us they do: race anyone.

#Luxembourg #Cycling

Braking on a downhill: squeeze both levers gently and early, rather than one lever hard and late.

Our hydraulic disc brakes need only light pressure, so there's no need to grip with all your strength. If you'd like to practise, our Steady Start lesson covers slopes.

Slow and steady stops well.

Summer slow ride: Diekirch to Echternach

On Sunday 25 August we're riding along the Sûre from Diekirch to Echternach, about 25 km on a flat cycle path. We'll stop for lunch in Echternach and come back by minibus, with the bikes on a trailer.

You're welcome on any bike, electric or not. If you don't have one, we can lend you a Stroller or a Sunday Best, but we only have ten, so please book early.

The pace will be gentle. Our ride leader has strict instructions to stop at anything interesting, which on this route is quite a lot.

Jean-Paul and Anne ride their Sunday Bests to Remich once a week, along the Moselle.

'We tried faster bikes,' Jean-Paul says. 'We spent the whole time concentrating. Now we talk.'

Anne adds that he still insists on leading. Some things a motor can't change.

A five-minute autumn check

Before the weather turns, give your bike a quick look over.

Tyres: press with your thumb; they should feel firm. Brakes: squeeze each lever; it should stop firmly well before it touches the handlebar. Lights: switch the bike on and check front and rear. Chain: if it's dry or squeaky, add a few drops of chain oil, then wipe off the extra. Bolts: if anything rattles, bring it in.

If that sounds like more than you'd like to do, that's what we're here for. Book a check at the showroom and we'll do it while you have a coffee.

Autumn is the best season for slow riding. The light is soft, the paths are quiet and the leaves are worth looking at.

One thing to watch: wet leaves are slippery. Ride around them rather than over them, and give yourself more room to stop.

At our speeds, that room comes easily.

Six months ago we opened our showroom in Bertrange with three test bikes and a kettle.

Since then we've added a second kettle. More importantly, we've met a great many people who wanted to keep riding but not to rush.

Thank you for every test ride, every cup of tea and every story. We're glad you're here.

What our customers do with the Sunday Best

When we launched the Sunday Best, we thought of it as a weekend bike. Our customers had other ideas. They ride it to the market, to see grandchildren and, in one case, to every meeting of a local history society.

Its upright position lets you see the road ahead without craning your neck. The motor helps up to 18 km/h, and it goes up to 80 km on a full charge.

If you'd like to try one, test rides at our Bertrange showroom are free. Drop in, or ring ahead and we'll have one ready.

Can I ride in the rain?

Yes. The electrics are rated IPX5, so our bikes can be ridden in the rain. Brake earlier and more gently than usual, and avoid painted lines and metal covers, which get slippery. After a wet ride, wipe the bike down and oil the chain once it's dry. Please don't use a pressure washer.

Your new Moien Vëlo bike gets its first service free after three months.

We check the brakes, the gears, the tyres and the battery, and we tighten anything that has settled. It takes about an hour, and you're welcome to wait with a coffee.

Reliable bikes need a little looking after. So do we all.

A word about brakes, because they matter more than motors.

Every bike we make has hydraulic disc brakes. They need only light pressure from your fingers, and they slow you smoothly rather than suddenly.

We'd rather spend money on stopping than on going.

The clocks have gone back, so the evenings are dark early.

Our bikes have front and rear lights built in, powered by the main battery. They come on when you switch the bike on, so there's nothing extra to fit. A light-coloured jacket helps too.

Be seen, ride slowly, get home.

Riding in the dark

Now that it's dark by five, a few habits make evening rides safer.

Your lights are built in and come on when you switch the bike on, so that's one thing taken care of. Add something bright or reflective to wear: a jacket, a vest or a pair of reflective bands around your ankles, which move as you pedal and catch drivers' eyes.

Stick to routes you know well and that are lit. Ride a little slower than usual, which on our bikes is saying something.

And if you'd rather not ride in the dark at all, that's a perfectly sensible choice. Mornings are lovely too.

Winter riding is possible, but we're not going to pretend it's pleasant every day.

On dry, bright mornings, wrap up and go. On icy ones, stay in and read about cycling instead. There's no shame in a day off. Your bike will still be here, charged and ready.

Tip: bring the battery indoors on cold nights. It prefers the warm.

Our first year

We opened in March with three test bikes. Since then we've held six slow rides, served what our accountant describes as 'too much tart' and learnt a great deal from you.

The question we hear most often is still: 'Isn't it a bit slow?' Our answer hasn't changed. It's slow on purpose. You have more time to react, less distance to stop and more chance to notice the view.

Thank you for riding with us this year. The showroom closes from 24 December to 2 January. We'll see you in the new year, at a sensible pace.

From all of us at Moien Vëlo: happy Christmas, and thank you for a gentle first year.

The showroom closes from 24 December to 2 January. If you need help with your bike in the meantime, leave us a message and we'll ring you back when we're open.

A gentler kind of New Year's resolution

If you've promised yourself more exercise this year, we'd like to offer a resolution you might actually keep: ride somewhere you'd normally drive, once a week.

It doesn't need to be far. The bakery, the post office or a friend's house will do. Choose a dry day, pick a low assist level if you're feeling ambitious and a high one if you're not.

You'll still be pedalling, and the motor will still be helping. We won't tell you which of you did more.

By March, you may find you've stopped thinking of it as exercise and started thinking of it as the nice way to get there.

January, when the rest of the world joins a gym.

We'd like to suggest an alternative. You sit down, you pedal gently, a small motor does much of the work, and you end up somewhere with cake. 🍰

We can't call that a fitness plan. We can call it a very nice morning.

People sometimes ask why we don't make a faster model.

We could. The parts exist and the law would allow it. But a bike that helps you up to 25 km/h needs more distance to stop than one that stops helping at 15. We'd rather give you more time to react, and more reasons to look around.

Slow is a feature, not a fault.

Winter storage, if you're taking a break

Not riding until spring? A little care now saves trouble later.

Clean the bike and dry it, especially the chain. Store it somewhere dry; a garage or cellar is fine. Take the battery indoors, charge it to about half and top it up once a month. Pump up the tyres before you put the bike away, and again before your first ride.

When spring comes, bring it in for a check if you like. We'll make sure everything is as you left it.

Henri, from Esch-sur-Alzette, had not been on a bicycle for thirty years when he came in for a test ride.

He went round the car park twice, very carefully. On the third lap he waved. He bought a Stroller that afternoon and now rides to his chess club on Thursdays.

He says the bike is slower than his opponents. We haven't asked him to explain.

Spring open day: Saturday 22 March

Our showroom in Bertrange is open from 10:00 to 16:00 for our spring open day.

You can test-ride every bike and see walk assist at work on our ramp. Our mechanics, Luc and Sandrine, will answer any question, from tyre pressure to saddle height. There will be coffee and homemade tart, as there always is.

No appointment is needed, and nobody will try to sell you anything you haven't asked about. Bring a friend who has been wondering whether an e-bike is for them.

Spring open day at our Bertrange showroom on Saturday 22 March, from 10:00 to 16:00.

Test-ride any bike in our range, ask our mechanics anything and have a slice of homemade tart. We'll also show you how walk assist helps when you're pushing the bike up a ramp.

No appointment needed.

Why we built slow bikes

When we started Moien Vëlo, people kept telling us the same thing: riders want speed. The legal limit for e-bikes is 25 km/h, and many use all of it.

We asked a different question. What do riders who've been away from cycling for a while actually need? The answer we kept hearing was confidence: time to look, time to think and time to stop.

So our motors stop helping at 15 or 18 km/h. A bike at 15 km/h needs less distance to stop than one at 25 km/h. That's physics, not marketing.

We don't want to get you there fast. We want to get you there alive.

Meet the Steady Eddie, our first e-trike.

Three wheels mean you don't have to balance when you stop, start or wait at a crossing. The motor helps up to 12 km/h, our most relaxed speed yet, and there's a large basket at the back for the shopping.

If balance is what has kept you off a bike, come and try it.

Steady Eddie

Our electric trike, for riders who want to cycle without thinking about balance. With two wheels at the back, it stays upright when you stop, so you can wait at a crossing without putting a foot down. The low frame and wide seat make getting on and off easy, and the rear basket takes a good-sized shop.

Motor assistance up to 12 km/h. Range up to 50 km. Weight 38 kg. Price €4,190.

What if I find a two-wheeled bike hard to balance?

The Steady Eddie trike may suit you. It has two wheels at the back and stays upright when you stop, so you don't need to put a foot down at junctions. It's a good way back into cycling if balance has been the obstacle.

Introducing the Steady Eddie

For some of you, the hardest part of cycling isn't the pedalling. It's the balance, especially when stopping and starting.

The Steady Eddie is our answer. It's an electric trike, with one wheel at the front and two at the back, so it stays upright when you stop. You can wait at a crossing without putting a foot down. The step-through frame is low and the seat is wide.

The motor helps up to 12 km/h, our gentlest speed, and the battery takes you up to 50 km. It costs €4,190, and test rides at the showroom are free.

If you gave up cycling because of balance, this might be the bike that brings you back.

Luxembourg is many things. Flat is not one of them.

The Gentle Climber has a stronger motor, with 85 Nm of torque, for the hills between you and the bakery. It still stops helping at 18 km/h, so it climbs with you rather than racing off.

The hill doesn't get smaller. It just stops being a reason to stay at home.

Gentle Climber

Made for Luxembourg's hills. The Gentle Climber's motor delivers 85 Nm of torque, so steep roads feel far more manageable, while assistance still stops at a sensible 18 km/h. A 625 Wh battery gives you up to 70 km.

Weight: 27 kg. Price: €3,890.

Introducing the Gentle Climber

Luxembourg has a lot of hills, and many of you have told us they're the reason you don't ride more.

The Gentle Climber has a stronger motor, with 85 Nm of torque, so it helps much more on steep roads. Like all our bikes, it still stops helping at a sensible speed, in this case 18 km/h. It climbs with you; it doesn't sprint off without you.

It has a 625 Wh battery and a range of up to 70 km, and it costs €3,890. If you live at the top of a hill, or want to visit someone who does, come and try one.

Before you ride, a quick check we call ABC: air in the tyres, brakes that bite, chain that's clean.

It takes a minute, and it's a minute well spent. If anything feels wrong, don't ride. Bring the bike to us instead and we'll put it right.

This month's ride: the Moselle from Remich to Schengen

Distance: about 11 km each way. Gradient: flat. Scenery: vineyards on one side, river on the other.

The cycle path runs right along the water and is well surfaced. Start in Remich, where there's parking near the promenade, and ride south to Schengen, where you can visit the small museum about the European agreement signed there.

The round trip suits every bike in our range. If the wine tasting in Schengen tempts you, remember that you're riding home. Have a coffee instead and come back for the wine another day.

Thérèse, from Diekirch, stopped cycling after a fall seven years ago. Last month she bought a Steady Eddie.

'I don't wobble,' she said, which we think is the best review a trike can get.

She now rides a loop of the park every morning and reports that the ducks have started to recognise her.

Gentle Effort mode

Level 5, our highest assist level. Pedal lightly and the motor adds up to four times your own effort, so hills, headwinds and long days feel far easier. You're still pedalling, so you're still riding. How hard you're working is between you and the bike.

Walk assist

Pushing your bike up a ramp, a steep driveway or a gravel path? Hold the walk assist button and the motor moves the bike at up to 6 km/h while you walk alongside. It's fitted to every model we make.

Hydraulic disc brakes

Every Moien Vëlo bike has hydraulic disc brakes. They need only light pressure on the levers and slow you smoothly and steadily, rather than with a jolt. We think brakes matter more than motors, so we never economise on them.

Built-in lights

Front and rear lights are built into every bike and powered by the main battery. They come on when you switch the bike on, so there's nothing to fit, charge or switch on separately.

Step-through frames

All our two-wheeled bikes have a low step-through frame. You step through the middle rather than swinging a leg over the saddle, which makes getting on and off easier, especially in a long coat or after a long lunch.

Built and checked in Bertrange

Every bike is assembled by our mechanics, then given a 40-point check and a test ride before it reaches you. Brakes, gears, lights, assist levels and every bolt are checked by the person who built it. If anything isn't right, the bike doesn't leave the workshop.

Our team

We're a small team of riders, mechanics and tea-makers. Luc and Sandrine build and service every bike. The rest of us answer the phone, deliver bikes, lead the slow rides and make sure there's always tart on open days. Between us, we've ridden a great many kilometres, none of them in a hurry.

What is Gentle Effort mode?

It's level 5, the highest of our five assist levels. Pedal lightly and the motor adds up to four times your own effort. It's ideal for hills, headwinds and days when you'd rather arrive fresh.

Three things people notice the first time they ride a Steady Eddie:

It stays upright when you stop. The seat is wide and the step is low. And the rear basket takes a good-sized shop, which is either a feature or a warning.

The motor helps up to 12 km/h, gently.

Choosing the right assist level

Your bike has five assist levels. Level 1 adds a little help. Level 5, which we call Gentle Effort mode, adds up to four times your own effort.

A rough guide: level 1 or 2 on flat roads if you'd like to work a bit, level 3 for everyday riding, and Gentle Effort mode for hills, headwinds and days when you'd simply rather not.

Lower levels use less battery, so you'll go further on a charge. Higher levels get you home with energy to spare.

There's no right answer. Customers who tell us they always use level 2 are, we suspect, being a little optimistic.

Our summer slow ride goes to Echternach on Sunday 29 June: 25 km along the Sûre, flat all the way, with lunch at the end.

Bikes are available to borrow, but please book, as we only have twelve. Our ride leader has one rule: nobody overtakes the ride leader.

Book in the showroom or by phone.

Thérèse and the ducks

Thérèse lives in Diekirch and stopped cycling seven years ago after a fall. She came to us in April 'just to look' at the Steady Eddie.

She rode it round the showroom car park, then round it again, then out onto the road before anyone could suggest otherwise. She bought it that afternoon.

Now she rides a loop of the park by the Sûre every morning. She says she doesn't wobble, she doesn't worry about stopping, and the ducks have learnt the sound of her bell.

'I missed this,' she told us. We were glad to help her find it again.

A short guide to looking sporty on a Moien Vëlo bike:

Wear a cycling jacket. Arrive slightly pink in the face. Say 'I did about 20 km' and leave it there.

Nobody needs to know which assist level you were on. Your secret is safe with us.

Every bike leaves our workshop after a 40-point check and a test ride by the mechanic who built it.

That ride is slow, naturally. It's also thorough: brakes, gears, lights, assist levels and a listen for any rattle that shouldn't be there.

If it isn't right, it doesn't leave.

Test rides at home

We'll bring two or three bikes to your door, anywhere in Luxembourg, so you can try them on the roads you actually ride. There's no charge and no obligation to buy. Book by phone or at the showroom.

Can I try a bike before I buy?

Of course. Test rides are free, at our showroom in Bertrange or at your home anywhere in Luxembourg. For a home test ride, we'll bring two or three bikes so you can compare them.

Test rides at home are now available anywhere in Luxembourg.

We bring two or three bikes to your door, you try them on roads you know, and there's no obligation to buy. Many people find it easier to decide on their own street than in a car park.

Test rides at your door

From this month, you can test-ride our bikes at home, anywhere in Luxembourg.

Tell us which models interest you and we'll bring two or three to your door. You try them on roads you know, up the hill you actually live on, at whatever pace suits you. There's no charge and no obligation.

We started this because so many of you said the same thing: a car park isn't the real world. Your own street is. Book by phone or in the showroom.

Hot weather and batteries don't mix. On very warm days, park in the shade and don't leave the battery charging in a sunny window.

You, likewise, should park in the shade. Ride early, carry water and take the café stop seriously.

This month's ride: Grund to Clausen, the lower town loop

Distance: about 5 km. Gradient: flat in the valley, with one optional climb. Cafés: many.

Start in the Grund, by the river, and follow the Alzette past the old abbey to Clausen. The paths are shared with walkers, so ride slowly, which you were going to do anyway.

If you'd like to finish in the upper town, set your bike to Gentle Effort mode and take the climb steadily. There's no rush at the top either.

A short ride, but a lovely one, especially early on a September morning.

Delivery from Moien Vëlo means we bring your new bike to your door anywhere in Luxembourg, set it up for your height and stay until you're comfortable on it.

We adjust the saddle, the handlebars and the brake levers, and we take you for a first short ride on your own street. Then we leave you to it.

Wet-weather riding

Autumn rain brings a few extra hazards: wet leaves, slippery painted lines and metal covers, and drivers who can't see as well.

Give yourself more room to stop. Brake earlier and more gently than usual, using both levers. Ride around leaves and puddles rather than through them, since you can't see what's under the water.

After a wet ride, wipe the bike down and put a few drops of oil on the chain once it's dry. Please don't use a pressure washer, however tempting.

Wet roads add metres to your stopping distance, at any speed.

On rainy days, start braking earlier and avoid painted lines and metal drain covers, which get slippery. Our lower top speeds give you a head start, but the rest is down to good habits.

Paul lives at the top of a hill in Vianden. For years he drove everywhere, because cycling home meant pushing.

He bought a Gentle Climber in September. 'I still get off at the very top,' he says, 'but only to admire the castle.'

We'll accept that.

Battery take-back

When your e-bike battery reaches the end of its life, bring it to our showroom. We'll take it back and send it to a specialist recycler, free of charge. You don't need to buy a new battery from us.

We've started a battery take-back scheme. When your e-bike battery reaches the end of its life, bring it to the showroom and we'll send it to a specialist recycler, free of charge.

It's a small thing, but batteries shouldn't end up in the household bin, and we'd rather you didn't have to work out where else they go.

Our battery take-back scheme

Sooner or later, every e-bike battery reaches the end of its useful life. When yours does, please don't put it in the household bin.

Bring it to our showroom in Bertrange instead. We'll take it back and send it to a specialist recycler, free of charge. You don't need a receipt, and you don't need to buy a replacement from us.

We'd rather tell you exactly what we do than use a vague label, because we think you'd rather know the details.

Our mechanics have an unofficial test for every new bike. They ride it to the bakery and back. If the croissants survive the journey in the basket, the bike passes.

We haven't had a failure yet. We have had a great many croissants.

A quiet word about winter

We'll be honest with you, as usual: winter isn't the best time for cycling, and nobody should feel obliged.

On bright, dry, frost-free days, wrap up well and enjoy the empty paths. On icy days, leave the bike at home. Our bikes are slow and steady, but no bike grips ice.

Paul's hill

Paul lives in Vianden, at the top of a road so steep that, for twenty years, he didn't cycle at all. 'Going down was fine,' he says. 'Coming back was a walk.'

In September he tried a Gentle Climber on a home test ride, up his own hill. He reached the top, turned round and rode up it again, just to be sure.

He now rides down to the river every morning for his newspaper and back up for breakfast. He gets off at the very top, he says, but only to look at the castle.

We've decided to believe him.

New Year's resolutions, ranked by how likely you are to keep them:

2. Try a slightly longer route.
3. Use a lower assist level.

We'll be honest: most people keep the first two.

Which bike is right for you?

For short trips around town, choose the Stroller or the Café Racer. If you'd like to ride further, the Sunday Best goes up to 80 km on a charge. If you live among hills, the Gentle Climber's stronger motor makes them manageable. And if balance is a concern, the Steady Eddie trike stays upright when you stop.

Our top assisted speeds

Every bike we make stops helping well below the EU limit of 25 km/h.

Café Racer: 10 km/h.
Steady Eddie: 12 km/h.
Stroller: 15 km/h.
Sunday Best: 18 km/h.
Gentle Climber: 18 km/h.

You can pedal faster on your own if you wish. The motor simply stops helping.

Why our bikes are slow

The law allows electric bikes to assist you up to 25 km/h. Ours stop helping at between 10 and 18 km/h, because a slower bike needs less distance to stop and gives you more time to react to whatever is ahead. It also gives you more time to enjoy the ride.

We don't want to get you there fast. We want to get you there alive.

How far can I ride on one charge?

It depends on the bike, the assist level, the hills and the wind. Our ranges, measured at the lowest assist level, run from up to 40 km on the Café Racer to up to 80 km on the Sunday Best. Higher assist levels use more battery.

Is the bike heavy?

Our bikes weigh between 22 kg (Café Racer) and 38 kg (Steady Eddie trike). That's heavier than a bicycle without a motor, so every model has walk assist to help when you're pushing it. If you need to lift a bike often, the Café Racer is the lightest.

Heat and your battery

Batteries dislike heat almost as much as some of our customers do.

In summer, park in the shade when you can. Don't charge the battery in direct sun or straight after a long ride on a hot day; let it cool for half an hour first. If you're not riding for a while, store it somewhere cool and dry.

The same advice applies to riders: shade, rest and plenty of water. Ride early or late, and don't feel you need to prove anything to anyone at two in the afternoon.

'Not really.'
'Will I get tired?'
'Only if you want to.'

That's the whole sales pitch, really. If you'd like to hear it in person, test rides are free and the kettle is usually on.

Summer reminder: in the heat, ride before 11:00 or after 17:00, carry water and keep the assist level up. There's no prize for suffering.

If you feel unwell, stop, find some shade and rest for a while. The bike is happy to wait, and so is the café.

In praise of Gentle Effort mode

Gentle Effort mode is level 5, our highest assist level. Pedal lightly and the motor adds up to four times your own effort.

Some people feel they ought to use it only on hills. We'd like to give you permission to use it whenever you like: into a headwind, on hot days, after lunch, or simply because you'd rather arrive fresh.

You're still pedalling. You're still out in the air, still riding, still getting there with a little help. That's what the bike is for.

New rules on environmental claims, and why we welcome them

From 27 September 2026, an EU law bans vague environmental claims in advertising. That includes Luxembourg. A company can no longer say a product is good for the planet in general terms unless it can prove it to a high standard. Claims based on carbon offsetting are banned too.

We've always tried to say only what we can prove. So we'll keep giving you specific facts. Our frames contain at least 60% recycled aluminium, checked by our supplier. And we take back old batteries for recycling, free of charge.

If you ever see a claim from us that you think we can't back up, please tell us.

Autumn leaves, wet roads and early dusk all arrive at once in October.

Ride in daylight where you can, brake early and gently, and keep to the middle of the cycle path, away from the leaf piles at the edges. Your built-in lights come on with the bike, which helps.

Getting ready for darker evenings

The clocks go back on 25 October. Before they do, check that your lights work: switch the bike on and look at the front and back.

Add a reflective jacket or ankle bands. Plan routes that are lit and that you know well. And if you can, move your regular ride to the morning.

If a light isn't working, bring the bike in. It's usually a loose connection and quick to fix.

Because we've chosen not to. Our motors stop helping at 20 km/h or less, below the legal limit of 25 km/h. A slower bike needs less distance to stop and gives you more time to react. You can still pedal faster if you want to; the motor simply won't help.
